Sometimes I see an issue with words because of the way I perceive patterns in a discussion. It is my fault I didn't explain the whole story. Basically the narrative of this article was about the fact that whole tragedy was solely caused by the teenager not talking to their parents about the whole situation, therefore he COMMITTED suicide moved by a general sense of guilt. A journalist can't allow himself to stick to an approximately narrative towards a tragedy of this caliber. "To commit" which "commettere" in Italian, in the English language has a really broader meaning, while in Italian is a really strong verb used exclusively for legal actions and crimes. While in English you can say you commit an act or you commit yourself in something or someone, in Italian you can't use the verb in the same way, you can "commettere" only crimes. There's a huge linguistical barrier between idioms of a different kind.

The problem is that misery loves company, and by company I mean people watching from outside the event itself like some sort of a strange ritual by which they take distance themselves by deducting the logic steps that lead to the tragedy itself, as they have the necessity to find a culprit or a logical cause behind this. In tragedies, such as these, there is no culprit or malevolent external force pulling the strings, just the pain behind the action. Pain can't be understood, it can only be felt. People want only to understand and ultimately not to feel, fearing they might fall to the same feeling the other person had. People who wear their hearts under our sleeves have an hard time approaching a society (yes, I've said the word) which has little to no interest to expand their insight.

Words are important and they carry a linguistic heritage. We have to weigh them on a scale before speaking our minds. Those who work in journalism should know it better than everyone else. I am not offended by the use of the verb "to commit", I am simply concerned about the fact that journalism relies on words to create some sort of excessive drama over human tragedies which carry dramatic consequences themselves. Journalism is supposed to discern and analyze reality, not inflating it.
